This course is primarily designed for international students in the CSPA English-language programme. Nevertheless, all undergraduate and graduate students who are interested in reading Japanese classics in English are warmly welcome to enroll. Students who wish to take the course are expected to attend the first session（Oct. 8).
＊本演習は、主にCSPAプログラムの留学生を対象としています。しかし、英語で小熊英二『単一民族神話の起源――〈日本人〉の自画像の系譜』を読みたい、また英語で議論してみたいと考えているすべての学部生・大学院生を歓迎します。受講希望者は、初回の授業(10月8日）に必ず参加してください。
授業概要
本講義は、小熊英二『単一民族神話の起源――〈日本人〉の自画像の系譜』を主要テキストとして、19世紀末から戦後にかけての日本人アイデンティティの構築と変容を検討する。「混合民族論」と「単一民族論」という日本人起源をめぐる二つの言説の歴史的展開と、それらが時代ごとの政治的文脈の中でどのように動員されてきたかを考察する。
This course examines how Japanese national self-identity was constructed and transformed from the late nineteenth century through the postwar period, using Oguma Eiji's "A Genealogy of 'Japanese' Self-images" as the primary text. Students will trace historical debates between theories of Japanese origins emphasizing racial mixture and those emphasizing national homogeneity, and examine how these theories were mobilized for different political purposes in changing historical contexts.

（内容）
Each week, one assigned student presents a summary and critical reflections of the reading (approx. 30 minutes). All other participants submit a short paper (approx. 1 page). Both the presenter's materials and the papers must be submitted in advance of the session. The remainder of the session is devoted to full-class discussion based on these submissions.

全体の教育目標
Through this course, students are expected to:
⚫︎Explain the historical development of theories of Japanese origins emphasizing racial mixture and those emphasizing national homogeneity. .
⚫︎Analyze how theories of national origin were mobilized for different political purposes across changing historical contexts.
⚫︎Critically evaluate primary and secondary sources on Japanese national identity discourse.
⚫︎Present research findings clearly and engage constructively in scholarly discussion.

授業の進め方
The course will be conducted primarily through student presentations and class discussions. For each session:
⚫︎ The presenting student will provide a summary of the assigned reading, investigate historical and conceptual background, and explain key vocabulary. Students are required to submit, via Moodle, a report of any length that includes their analysis and critical reflections in advance.
⚫︎ Other students are expected to submit a one-page(approximately 300-400 words) reflection on the reading prior to class via Moodle. These reflections should engage critically with the text and help facilitate in-class discussion.
⚫︎ Class time will be devoted to presentations, peer feedback, and guided discussion.
